prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength enable frequency standards at the 10^-18 level and the study of many-body effects within a clock

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from B006 to B024, and I want to say why in physical terms and not as deference to a count. The decisive point for me is the one Kroll and Lindroth made against my round-1 worry about overlap: the 2005 comb is a ruler for optical frequencies and the 2012 ion work is control of single quantum systems, whereas Katori's idea is a specific mechanism. Choosing the trap wavelength so that the light shifts of the two clock levels cancel removes the one effect that otherwise forbids tight confinement of neutral atoms, and that single condition is what turns one interrogated ion into thousands of atoms and gains orders of magnitude in statistical power. It is the kind of simple, general mechanism I look for, it is understood and not merely engineered, and it has been reproduced at the 10^-18 level by several independent groups with different species. Ye's group then showed what the idea can do, including the study of interactions and many-body effects inside the clock, which is physics and not only systematics control. Two names cover the invention and its realization with no gap that anyone in the committee has named, and the citation can be written entirely on what has been demonstrated, without relying on a redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: My remaining reservation is the one I raised in round 1 and which still stands: B024 is a quantitative leap in an existing capability, and some of the physics it enables (tests of constants, relativistic geodesy, dark matter) is promised more than delivered. The committee should be honest that it is rewarding an invention and its realization, not a new phase or a new law. Priority is also not perfectly tidy: Takamoto and Katori's 2005 demonstration, Lemonde at SYRTE, and Ludlow, Hinkley and others at NIST hold real claims to particular milestones that two names pass over. I also still cannot cleanly separate Katori's concept from Ye's record accuracy, and the citation must say what each is being credited for. On my former choice B006: I now think the case is not strong enough for 2026. Yuhai Tu, who is coauthor of the central continuum theory, is outside any three-name credit, and the Toner-Tu exponents are tested well by numerical work but only partially by experiment. This is a statement about timing and credit, not about the quality of the physics.

responses.point: He argues that the lattice clock is a different invention from the comb because it needs the magic-wavelength condition, many-atom interrogation and years of systematics work, and that the redefinition of the second argues for recognizing the work now.
responses.response: This is what changed my mind on the overlap. I had treated the lattice clock as a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 lineage, but the magic-wavelength condition is a separate mechanism with a separate consequence, which is the large atom number. I do not agree that the pending redefinition argues for timing; I would leave it out of the citation entirely, as you and Lindroth also propose. I accept your point that the many-body physics Ye's group developed belongs in the case, and I would put it in the citation as a clause, not as the headline. My remaining question for you is whether you would want the citation to separate Katori's proposal from Ye's accuracy work, or let one clause cover both.

responses.point: She presses on whether the many-body and interaction physics in the clock belongs in the citation, and resists extending the credit beyond two names to SYRTE and NIST contributors.
responses.response: I agree with both points. The clock-interaction work is what makes this physics and not engineering to a statistical physicist, since it is a controlled many-body problem with a measurable frequency shift. On credit, I would not extend beyond Katori and Ye: the three-name limit does not allow a fair expansion, and the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow are real but are milestones inside the lineage, not an alternative origin of the idea. I would ask that the final record state this limit openly, so that the omission is a conscious decision and not an oversight. I also note that your answer to my round-1 note, that you defer to me on B006, was fair; I return it, since the atomic-physics judgments here are yours.

responses.point: He asks whether the Toner-Tu exponents have been tested quantitatively in experiments, and says a theoretical framework with only partial experimental tests sits less comfortably with him than a result reproduced across laboratories.
responses.response: The chair asked the same question, and I owe a direct answer, with the caveat that I am working from memory and have not checked the sources. Giant number fluctuations, a robust consequence of the theory, have been measured in vibrated granular rods and in bacterial and colloidal suspensions, and long-range order in 2D polar flocks has been studied in simulation with exponents close to the Toner-Tu values. But no experiment, to my recollection, has measured the full set of scaling exponents with the precision that clock comparisons give routinely, and Vicsek-type models also show a first-order character in some regimes. So your discomfort is justified and it is one reason I am moving. I also take your earlier point on B003: I share your maturity concern about the unsettled superconducting mechanism.

responses.point: He ranks B003 first and says he would be content to see B024 first if the committee decides the moire field needs more time; the chair also asks whether dropping Bistritzer, as I suggested, is acceptable.
responses.response: I want to withdraw my own suggestion on Bistritzer. The Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction is the theory-leads-experiment element that makes B003 persuasive, and removing its first author weakens the very argument you make, while the real credit gap is on the experimental side with Cao, Dean, Young, Yazdani and Efetov, which no three-name list repairs. My view on your question about mechanism is that an open pairing mechanism is not by itself a bar, since the committee has honored discoveries before they were fully explained. It is for me a reason to wait a few years until sample dependence and twist-angle disorder are better controlled and the experimental credit is clearer. I therefore keep B003 as my second alternative and I thank you for the generous position on B024.

responses.point: As chair he places B024 first with a clean two-person credit and notes the pending redefinition of the second without making it a condition, and he asks for the citation to avoid relying on it.
responses.response: I agree with the framing and would add one point about wording. The citation should name the lattice scheme and its realization at 10^-18, and should not claim that the second has been redefined or imply that the prize rests on metrological adoption. I also think a two-part prize with B003 is not available under the three-person limit, since Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer would be five names. I would not want to cut the credit to make a combination fit.

uncertainties: I am working from memory on priority dates, the history of the Sr, Yb and Hg lattice clocks, and the experimental record for Toner-Tu scaling; none has been checked against sources.
I cannot judge from outside atomic physics whether Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow or Hinkley hold a claim that two names would be unfair to omit, and I rely on Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson on this.
Whether Katori's concept and Ye's realization should be credited jointly or separated in the citation, and whether the many-body clause strengthens or dilutes it.
Whether B006 would be ready in a later year once quantitative experimental tests exist and the credit question around Yuhai Tu is addressed.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate. I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye. I co-wrote a 2020 review on machine learning for active matter, which is a mild connection to B006 only, with no collaboration with Vicsek, Toner or Ramaswamy. Eva Olsson and Goran Johansson are in the same Gothenburg physics environment, which is an institutional fact and not a collaboration, and I am not aware of any relationship that changes my weighing of B024.
